prompt: In politics, what does suffrage mean?
answers: The right to vote
The power to collect taxes
The duty to serve in the army
The right to issue currency
rationale: Suffrage is voting right. Tax powers, military service and currency issue not synonyms. Election scope explicit, ordinary British wording correct; actual dictionary suffrage definition inspected.

prompt: What is a referendum?
answers: A direct public vote on a particular question
A vote held only by cabinet ministers
A court ruling on a disputed law
A private vote to elect a party leader
rationale: Referendum direct public question vote, not cabinet-only vote, judicial ruling or internal party leadership ballot. Improve distractors to real civic procedures. No claim all referendums are legally binding.

prompt: What is a ballot paper used for in an election?
answers: Recording a voter's choice
Listing the policies of every party
Showing the final result of the count
Recording a candidate's campaign expenses
rationale: Ballot-paper sense records voter's choice. Policy document, final results and expense return different documents. Read paper sense rather than investment-share allotment sense; apostrophe voter's correct.

prompt: Where do voters go to cast their votes in person on election day?
answers: A polling station
A constituency surgery
A cabinet meeting
A party selection meeting
rationale: Polling station is in-person voting place. Constituency surgery,cabinet,selection meeting not election-day voting site. No claim postal/proxy voters must attend; wording explicitly in person.

prompt: What does a political party's election manifesto usually set out?
answers: Its policies and plans if elected
The final vote count in every constituency
A confidential record of cabinet discussions
A list of all eligible voters
rationale: Manifesto sets policies/plans. Vote counts,confidential minutes,electoral roll different records. Usually permits parties publishing other material; possessive party's correct.

prompt: What is an incumbent politician?
answers: The person currently holding a particular office
The person selected to count votes
The candidate who finished second last time
The person reporting election news
rationale: Incumbent currently holds office. Vote counter,previous runner-up,reporter not definition. Relevant elected-position sense checked among duty/business meanings. Does not mean automatically seeking re-election.

prompt: What is a coalition government?
answers: A government formed by two or more political parties working together
A government with no ministers
A government that bans all elections
A government led by the courts alone
rationale: Coalition joins parties in governing. No-minister,banned-election,courts-only alternatives wrong. Two or more permits more than two and does not confuse minority single-party administration with coalition.

prompt: In a parliamentary system, which is a key role of the opposition?
answers: Challenging and scrutinising the government
Implementing the government's entire programme
Acting as the country's highest court
Appointing every civil servant
rationale: Opposition scrutiny/challenge is a key role. It does not implement government's entire programme,act as judiciary or appoint all civil servants. Key role replaces main to avoid oversimplifying multiple legitimate functions.

prompt: In government, what is a cabinet?
answers: A group of senior ministers
All the judges in the highest court
All the registered voters in one district
A group of foreign ambassadors
rationale: Cabinet senior ministers, not judiciary,electorate or foreign diplomatic corps. Political noun sense rather than furniture. Size and membership vary, so no universal number specified.

prompt: In an election, what is a constituency?
answers: An area whose voters elect a representative
A government's annual spending plan
A formal agreement between countries
A list of proposed changes to a bill
rationale: Constituency area electing representative. Budget,treaty,amendment list not geographic electoral units. Read area sense as well as voter/group meanings; question in an election supplies context.

prompt: In an election, who is a candidate?
answers: Someone seeking election to office
The official supervising the count
A voter who has already voted
A reporter announcing the result
rationale: Candidate seeks election. Supervisor,voter,reporter different roles; a candidate may also vote but a voter merely having voted does not define candidacy. Remove only-retired-judge distractor.

prompt: What are campaigners doing when they canvass voters?
answers: Seeking their support or opinions
Counting completed ballot papers
Drawing constituency boundaries
Swearing elected members into office
rationale: Canvassing seeks support/opinions. Counting votes,boundary setting,swearing-in different acts. Dictionary supports support and survey senses; not canvas fabric spelling.

prompt: When is an exit poll conducted?
answers: As voters leave the polling station after voting
Before the names of the candidates are announced
Only after the final official count is complete
Before a voter has cast a ballot
rationale: Exit poll asks after vote as voters leave. Before ballot or candidate announcement wrong; only-after-final-count not exit polling. Change after voters leave to as they leave for precise timing.

prompt: What does an opinion poll try to measure?
answers: The views of a sample of people
The official final count of every vote
The exact outcome of every future election
Only the membership of the cabinet
rationale: Opinion poll samples views. It is not official complete count,certainty about future or cabinet membership. No claim sample is invariably representative or prediction accurate.

prompt: What does bipartisan cooperation involve?
answers: Cooperation between two political parties
A government formed without political parties
Cooperation restricted to one party's members
The merger of two courts
rationale: Bipartisan means two parties/both sides. No-party government,one-party-only cooperation,court merger not meaning. Does not require parties to merge or govern together.

prompt: What is a hung parliament?
answers: A parliament in which no party has an overall majority
A parliament in which every seat is vacant
A parliament with a single chamber
A parliament in which one party holds every seat
rationale: Hung parliament means no single-party overall majority, not empty seats,one chamber or one party owning every seat. Parliamentary rather than furniture meaning; remove sitting-outdoors joke option.

prompt: What is a UK parliamentary by-election normally held to do?
answers: Fill a seat that becomes vacant between general elections
Elect the monarch
Choose every MP at once
Appoint all Supreme Court judges
rationale: UK by-election fills vacancy between generals. Monarch and Supreme Court judges not elected this way; all-MP election is general. Normally qualifies uncontested/administrative edge cases without changing central meaning.

prompt: In UK politics, what does devolution involve?
answers: Transferring powers from central government to governments in parts of the country
Transferring powers from regional governments back to the centre
Transferring ownership of public businesses to private investors
Merging several countries into one state
rationale: UK devolution transfers powers away from centre to territorial institutions; reverse centralisation,privatisation,state merger distinct. Parliament glossary consulted because generic dictionary central-to-local wording too broad for precise UK devolved governments.

prompt: What is a central feature of federalism?
answers: Power is divided between a national government and constituent states or regions
All governing powers belong exclusively to local councils
All decisions must be made by direct referendum
The national government has no authority of its own
rationale: Federalism shares/divides authority among national and constituent levels. Only-local,no-national-authority and obligatory direct referendum not definitions. National Archives school lesson explicitly defines divided responsibilities; supersedes oversimplified dictionary first definition.

prompt: What does it mean if a legislature is bicameral?
answers: It has two chambers
It has two prime ministers
It sits only twice a year
It represents only two voters
rationale: Bicameral means two chambers. Two PMs,two yearly sittings,two voters unrelated counts. Parliament/congress scope explicit; not requirement that chambers have equal power.

prompt: How many chambers does a unicameral legislature have?
answers: One
Two
Three
Four
rationale: Unicameral one chamber;two/three/four wrong. Dictionary says only one group of members. No conflation with one-party government.

prompt: What is the main function of a legislature?
answers: Making laws
Conducting foreign diplomacy
Commanding military operations
Hearing appeals against criminal convictions
rationale: Legislature chiefly makes laws. Diplomacy,military command,criminal appeals are other functions. Main function qualifier accommodates oversight/tax approval and constitutional variations; replace retail/weather distractors.

prompt: In government, what does the executive branch mainly do?
answers: Puts laws and government policy into effect
Hears court cases and gives judgments
Acts as a chamber for debating proposed laws
Runs only the opposition's election campaign
rationale: Executive puts laws/policy into effect. Judicial judgments,legislative debating chamber,opposition campaign are different. Actual government noun sense inspected among corporate executive definitions.

prompt: What does the term judiciary refer to?
answers: The judges and courts of a legal system
The senior ministers in the cabinet
The elected members of a legislature
The staff of diplomatic missions
rationale: Judiciary judges/courts, not cabinet,legislature,diplomatic staff. Dictionary explicitly legal-system branch. Replace sports-team distractor; no assertion judges can never have any other public roles.

prompt: What does it mean to veto a proposed measure?
answers: Use an official power to reject or block it
Approve it without changes
Suggest a change while allowing it to proceed
Refer it to an opinion poll for advice
rationale: Veto official block/rejection, not approval,merely proposing amendment or advisory poll. Does not claim every veto is permanent or cannot be overridden; official power qualification important.

prompt: In US politics, impeachment of a federal official is what?
answers: A formal accusation of wrongdoing by the House of Representatives
Automatic removal from office without any further process
An ordinary general election
A grant of hereditary office
rationale: US House impeachment accusation differs from conviction/removal. Senate official account explicitly separates charges from trial/conviction. General election and heredity wrong; federal scope excludes differing state procedures.

prompt: What is a term of office?
answers: The period for which someone holds a public position
The area represented by an elected member
The number of votes needed to win a seat
The amount a candidate spends campaigning
rationale: Term period holding public office, not district,vote threshold or campaign cost. Relevant job/government period sense inspected among school/pregnancy/mathematical definitions; no universal fixed duration claimed.

prompt: What does it mean when a parliamentary meeting is adjourned?
answers: The meeting is suspended or ended until another time
Every member permanently loses their seat
The parliament is dissolved for a general election
A proposal automatically becomes law
rationale: Adjourn pauses/temporarily ends meeting. Members losing seats,dissolution,automatic lawmaking not it. Until another time preserves temporary nature; distinguishes dissolution and recess.

prompt: What is a parliamentary recess?
answers: A break when parliament is not sitting
The permanent end of a parliament before an election
A formal vote on a disputed motion
A meeting of the governing cabinet
rationale: Recess break in sitting, not end of Parliament,vote or cabinet meeting. Parliamentary noun sense checked, not school break/alcove. No claim members stop all constituency/committee work.

prompt: What is a quorum at a formal meeting?
answers: The minimum number of members required for valid business
The number of votes a proposal receives
The maximum number of speeches in a debate
The total number of seats held by the largest party
rationale: Quorum minimum required participants for valid business. Vote outcome,speech cap,largest-party seat count not meaning. No arbitrary universal numeric quorum invented.

prompt: What is an amendment to a proposed law?
answers: A change to its wording or provisions
The final official count of an election
A diplomatic agreement with another state
A list of people entitled to vote
rationale: Amendment change to proposed text/provisions. Count,treaty,electorate list not it. Proposed-law qualifier narrows legal meaning; relevant draft-law dictionary sense checked.

prompt: In a legislature, what is a bill?
answers: A proposal for a new law
A formal agreement between countries
A decision reached by a judge
A party's list of election promises
rationale: Bill proposed law, not treaty,judicial decision or manifesto. Legislative context excludes banknote,bird's bill,invoice and programme billing. More plausible civic distractors added.

prompt: What is a petition in public life?
answers: A formal request, often supported by signatures
A record of the final votes in an election
A list of government ministers
A formal agreement between states
rationale: Petition formal request often signed. Election result,minister list,treaty not it. Often allows parliamentary petitions presented through representative and other lawful forms; avoids arbitrary minimum signatures.

prompt: What does political lobbying involve?
answers: Trying to influence public decisions or decision-makers
Supervising the official count at an election
Delivering a court judgment
Appointing diplomatic staff
rationale: Lobbying seeks to influence decisions. Count supervision,judicial judgment,diplomatic appointments not definition. No suggestion lobbying necessarily illegal or always involves money.

prompt: What does a pressure group usually try to do?
answers: Influence policy on an issue or set of interests
Count ballots as the official election authority
Hear appeals as the highest court
Act as the government's permanent administration
rationale: Pressure group aims to influence policy/interests, unlike election authority,court,civil service. Usually accommodates different tactics; not claimed every pressure group becomes electoral party.

prompt: A grassroots political movement mainly develops from which level?
answers: Ordinary people at the local or community level
Only the national cabinet
Only senior judges
Only career diplomats overseas
rationale: Grassroots ordinary people/community, not exclusivelycabinet/judges/diplomats. Relevant people sense inspected. A politician may participate but top-down official control is not defining source.

prompt: In parliamentary politics, what is one role of a party whip?
answers: Helping organise party members' attendance and voting
Chairing the legislature impartially
Overseeing the national election count
Judging whether an accused official is guilty
rationale: Whip organises member attendance/party voting. Speaker,election counter,trial judge distinct. Actual political whip sense checked, not leather tool/food/car. One role qualifier allows welfare/communication duties.

prompt: In UK politics, what is a backbencher?
answers: An MP who is not a minister or an opposition frontbench spokesperson
The most senior judge
The head of every political party
An ambassador serving overseas
rationale: Backbench MP lacks ministerial or opposition frontbench spokesperson role. Judge,party head,ambassador not meaning. Parliament party-system text directly inspected to refine dictionary broad no-official-position formulation.

prompt: In the UK House of Lords, a Crossbencher is best described as what?
answers: An independent peer outside the party groups
A minister who represents all political parties
An elected member of the House of Commons
The official responsible for counting general-election votes
rationale: Crossbencher non-party peer outside party groups. Multi-party minister,Commons MP,election counter wrong. Cambridge guessed crossbencher entry had no definition; replace with Parliament explicit Crossbench Peers description. Do not assert every unwhipped peer is automatically a Crossbencher.

prompt: What is a parliamentary Speaker primarily responsible for during debates?
answers: Chairing proceedings and maintaining order
Writing the governing party's election manifesto
Counting votes at every public election
Leading negotiations with foreign governments
rationale: Speaker chairs debate/maintains order. Party-manifesto author,public election counter,diplomatic negotiator not defining job. Parliamentary sense checked beyond loudspeaker/orator; no claim all countries choose Speakers identically.

prompt: In the UK Parliament, what is a division?
answers: A formal vote
A party's election poster
A royal wedding
A judge's written sentence
rationale: Division formal parliamentary vote. Poster,royal wedding,court sentence not it. Cambridge entry did not cover parliamentary division; Parliament glossary explicitly describes counting for/against through lobbies.

prompt: What is a filibuster intended to do?
answers: Delay or obstruct legislative business through prolonged debate or other tactics
Speed every proposal into law automatically
Select candidates by lottery
Replace every voter with a judge
rationale: Filibuster delays/obstructs legislative business with speeches/rules. Automatic speed-through,candidate lottery,voter replacement wrong. Dictionary includes tactics as well as prolonged speeches; not overrestricted to one country.

prompt: What is gerrymandering?
answers: Manipulating electoral boundaries for political advantage
Counting votes in alphabetical order
Holding elections on a weekend
Giving every voter the same ballot paper
rationale: Gerrymandering manipulates electoral boundaries for advantage. Alphabetical counting,weekend voting,same ballot paper not it. No partisan accusation or current boundary opinion included.

prompt: What is proportional representation intended to make seats broadly reflect?
answers: Parties' shares of the vote
The length of time each party has existed
The total number of party members
The amount each party spends on posters
rationale: PR seats broadly reflect vote shares, not party age,membership or advertising. Broadly accommodates thresholds/rounding/formula differences. No claim perfect exact proportionality in every implementation.

prompt: Under first-past-the-post voting in a single-member constituency, who wins the seat?
answers: The candidate with the most votes
The candidate with the most first-time voters only
The candidate selected by the previous representative
The candidate whose party wins nationally, regardless of the local count
rationale: FPTP most votes in single-member seat. Not only first-time voters,named predecessor's pick or national winner regardless of local votes. Does not require more than half; specify local constituency to distinguish national totals.

prompt: What is a runoff election?
answers: A further round of voting to decide a winner
A recount of exactly the same ballot papers
An opinion poll before candidates are selected
A ceremony marking the start of a presidency
rationale: Runoff further voting round, not recount of same ballots,preselection survey,inauguration. Relevant electoral sense checked beyond water runoff. No single worldwide qualification threshold imposed.

prompt: In US elections, what is a party primary used to help choose?
answers: The party's candidate for an election
The final winner of the general election automatically
The official who supervises every ballot count
The person who chairs the Supreme Court
rationale: Primary helps choose party nominee, not automatically general-election winner,count supervisor or chief justice. Helps accommodates delegate/convention processes; relevant US political noun sense inspected beyond school/first/main.

prompt: In US presidential candidate selection, a caucus is typically what?
answers: A meeting of party members or supporters to express their preferences
A court hearing to settle a disputed election
An official recount of general-election ballots
A ceremony to swear in the president
rationale: Caucus candidate-selection meeting of party supporters,membership rules vary. Court,count,inauguration not it. Typically avoids claiming every caucus means only election meeting; legislative caucuses also exist.

prompt: What is a president's inauguration?
answers: The formal ceremony marking the start of the presidency
The selection of a party's election candidate
The official count on election night
The formal announcement of a president's retirement
rationale: Inauguration formal start ceremony, not nomination,count or retirement announcement. No claim inauguration alone is legal source of term start in all constitutions. President possessive correct.

prompt: In UK politics, what is the dissolution of Parliament?
answers: The formal end of a Parliament before a general election
A temporary break between parliamentary sittings
A reshuffle of cabinet ministers
A formal vote on a proposed law
rationale: UK dissolution formal Parliament end before general election. Temporary break,reshuffle,bill vote distinct. Jurisdiction narrowed and Parliament glossary used; avoid confusing prorogation/session end with entire Parliament end.

prompt: What is a head of state?
answers: The person who formally represents a country at the highest constitutional level
The chief organiser of every election campaign
The most senior newspaper editor
The representative of one local ward
rationale: Head of state formal highest representative;campaign organiser,editor,ward representative not definition. It can be monarch or president and executive or ceremonial, so no claim always powerless.

prompt: In the UK, which officeholder leads the government?
answers: The Prime Minister
The Speaker of the House of Commons
The Leader of the Opposition
The Lord Chief Justice
rationale: Guessed head-of-government dictionary entry lacked definition. Replace with concrete UK office: PM leads government. Speaker,opposition leader,Lord Chief Justice different roles. GOV.UK institutional description inspected; no current personal name used.

prompt: In a republic, the head of state is generally what?
answers: A person who is not a monarch
Always a hereditary king
Always a hereditary queen
Always the leader of a religious institution
rationale: Republic's head of state not monarch. Hereditary king/queen and always religious leader wrong. Remove hereditary-only wording from correct choice because elective monarchies remain monarchies; generally allows complex historical terminology without claiming every republic democratic.

prompt: In a constitutional monarchy, what limits the monarch's governing powers?
answers: A constitutional framework
The monarch's wishes alone
The personal rules of a royal servant
The views of one private company
rationale: Constitutional framework limits monarch's powers. Monarch's wishes alone/private servant/company not source of constitutional restrictions. Royal official explanation specifies Parliament's legislative role; do not assert every constitution must be one codified written document.

prompt: What characterises political absolutism?
answers: A ruler or ruling group holds complete governing power
The national government has no authority
Every policy is decided by direct public vote
Political authority is divided equally among all citizens
rationale: Absolute-monarchy guessed page only examples,no definition. Replace with political absolutism, dedicated Cambridge entry explicitly complete power by ruler/group/party. No-authority,direct-every-policy,equal citizen authority opposite concepts; do not confuse absolute with merely hereditary.

prompt: In a democracy, political authority is ultimately meant to come from whom?
answers: The people
Only one hereditary family
Only foreign ambassadors
Only the wealthiest corporation
rationale: Democratic authority meant to originate with people. Exclusivelydynasty,foreign ambassadors or corporation not principle. Ultimately meant to allows imperfect actual practice and avoids assessing disputed present-day regimes.

prompt: What distinguishes direct democracy from representative democracy?
answers: Citizens vote on policies or laws themselves
Citizens choose representatives to decide every policy for them
Citizens have no voting rights
Only the cabinet is allowed to vote
rationale: Direct democracy citizens decide policies/laws directly. Representation-only,no-voting,cabinet-only not defining. Different from58's representative route; no claim systems cannot combine both forms.

prompt: In a representative democracy, citizens normally make political choices by doing what?
answers: Electing people to make decisions on their behalf
Voting directly on every government decision
Allowing a monarch to appoint every representative
Letting judges choose all legislative members
rationale: Representative democracy elects decision-makers. Every direct decision,monarch appointment,judge appointment alternatives not electoral representation. Normally accommodates referendums alongside representative institutions.

prompt: What is an autocracy?
answers: A system concentrating power in a ruler or small ruling group
A system requiring every citizen to agree to each decision
A system with no governing authority
A system that distributes power equally to all citizens
rationale: Cambridge autocracy allows ruler or small group, so expand original one-ruler-only answer. Unanimous-all,equal-power-all,no-government not meaning. Avoid confusing narrow common singular-ruler usage with universal claim.

prompt: A dictatorship is typically characterised by what?
answers: Power concentrated in an authoritarian ruler or ruling group
Guaranteed open competition for every public office
No authority to enforce any rules
A requirement that every law be approved by a jury
rationale: Dictatorship authoritarian concentrated power. Guaranteed open competition,no enforcing authority,mandatoryjury-for-all-laws not characteristics. Typically recognises varying institutional forms; no present country labelled.

prompt: What is an oligarchy?
answers: Government or control by a small powerful group
Government through direct voting by the entire population
Government with no officials or institutions
Government controlled by every citizen equally
rationale: Oligarchy small powerful group. Whole-population direct rule,no institutions,equalallcitizens not definition. All options inspected; remove random child comic distractor.

prompt: In a theocracy, political authority is closely tied to what?
answers: Religious authority
Independent sporting bodies
Only commercial stock exchanges
Only public opinion surveys
rationale: Theocracy links political and religious authority. Sports bodies,stock exchange only,polls only wrong. Dictionary religious-leader rule checked; no assertion every religious country is theocracy.

prompt: What is a plutocracy?
answers: Rule or dominant political influence by the wealthy
Rule based only on military rank
Rule based only on religious office
Rule by citizens selected at random
rationale: Plutocracy wealthy dominance, not militaryrank/religiousoffice/randomcitizens as defining selection. Dominant influence permits informal as well as formal rule; no current political insinuation.

prompt: What is diplomacy in international relations?
answers: Managing relations between states through negotiation and communication
Drawing boundaries between local electoral wards
Counting ballots in a domestic election
Passing judgment in a domestic criminal case
rationale: Diplomacy manages interstate relations via communication/negotiation. Local boundaries,domestic counts,courtjudgments different. International relations scope excludes personal tact sense.

prompt: What is an ambassador?
answers: A senior diplomatic representative of a state
A tourist automatically granted political office
A candidate seeking election in every district
A judge who hears all international disputes
rationale: Ambassador senior diplomatic representative. Not automaticroyalstatus,candidate in everydistrict or all-disputejudge. Broaden answer beyond only another-country posting to allow ambassadors to international organisations.

prompt: What is an embassy?
answers: A state's diplomatic mission or its premises in another country
A court that hears every domestic criminal trial
A place that automatically becomes a new sovereign country
A private political party's campaign office
rationale: Embassy diplomatic mission/building. Not all-domestic court,new sovereign country or party office. Mission or premises wording reflects both dictionary senses; embassy land not magically separate sovereign state.

prompt: What is a treaty?
answers: A formal agreement between states
An unofficial television opinion
A single voter's choice on a ballot
A political party's internal campaign leaflet
rationale: Treaty formal interstate agreement. Presenter opinion,individual ballot,internalleaflet not treaty. Simplify specialist subjects-of-international-law wording to states without claiming treaties can never involve international organisations.

prompt: What does an armistice agreement provide for?
answers: A halt in fighting
A compulsory merger of the states involved
An automatic change of national leadership
A final settlement of every disputed issue
rationale: Armistice halt in fighting, not automaticmerger,leadershipchange or finalsettlementallissues. Dictionary explicitly temporary halt and possible peace talks. Distinguish armistice from permanent peace treaty.

prompt: What are international sanctions generally intended to do?
answers: Put pressure on a state or other target to change its behaviour
Guarantee unrestricted trade with the target
Recognise the target as a new sovereign state automatically
Give the target a seat in every international organisation
rationale: Sanctions pressure behaviour. Not necessarilyunrestrictedtrade,newstate recognition or universalseats. Relevant international punitive meaning inspected; sanction can mean approval in other contexts, hence international sanctions scope.

prompt: In politics, sovereignty concerns what?
answers: Supreme authority over a state or territory
The popularity of one governing party
The number of seats in a parliament
The size of a diplomatic delegation
rationale: Sovereignty supreme governing authority. Party popularity,seatcount,delegationsize not it. Supreme authority wording within politics, not a claim no international obligations can exist.

prompt: A multilateral agreement involves how many parties?
answers: More than two
Exactly one
Exactly two
None
rationale: Multilateral more than two participants, not one/two/none. Dictionary explicit more than two. Parties means participating states/entities, not necessarily political parties.

prompt: A bilateral agreement is between how many parties?
answers: Two
Three
Four
Ten
rationale: Bilateral two parties, not three/four/ten. Same international-agreement meaning distinct from multilateral. No claim parties must be countries rather than organisations.

prompt: Domestic policy mainly concerns what?
answers: Matters directly affecting people within a country
Only relations with foreign governments
Only the work of embassies overseas
Only treaties between military allies
rationale: Domestic policy matters directly affecting people within country. Foreigngovernments-only,embassies-only,militarytreaties-only wrong. Direct-effects wording more faithful than rigid border claim; domestic policy may have external effects too.

prompt: Foreign policy concerns a state's approach to what?
answers: Other countries and international affairs
Only the organisation of local refuse collection
Only the management of domestic school admissions
Only the opening hours of local libraries
rationale: Foreign policy dealings with other states/international affairs. Onlylocalrefuse,domesticschooladmissions,libraryhours not definition. Scope avoids saying trade/defence are the only elements.

prompt: Fiscal policy mainly concerns which government tools?
answers: Taxation and public spending
Interest rates and money supply alone
The drawing of electoral boundaries
The appointment of ambassadors
rationale: Fiscal taxation/publicspending, not money-supply/interestrates alone,electoral maps,ambassadors. Dictionary fiscalplan checked. Government borrowing also fiscal but answer lists maintools, not exhaustivealltools.

prompt: Monetary policy mainly concerns what?
answers: Money supply and the cost of borrowing
Only the boundaries of constituencies
Only the selection of election candidates
Only the appointment of cabinet ministers
rationale: Monetary policy money supply/costofborrowing. Constituencies,candidates,cabinetappointment not it. Does not claim politicians personally set rates everywhere; neutral financial-policy concept fits Politics.

prompt: What is a government budget?
answers: A plan for public income and spending
A list of all election candidates
A record of treaties with other countries
A map of local government areas
rationale: Government budget income/spending plan. Candidate list,treaty register,wardmap different. Relevant financial/UKgovernment senses inspected, not low-price adjective or time budget.

prompt: A government budget deficit occurs when what happens?
answers: Spending exceeds revenue
Revenue exceeds spending
Spending and revenue are exactly equal
No public money is spent or collected
rationale: Deficit spending exceeds revenue. Opposite surplus,equalbalanced,nothingcollectedorspent wrong. Government budget context excludes trade/current-account deficits; not confused with total debt.

prompt: A government budget surplus occurs when what happens?
answers: Revenue exceeds spending
Spending exceeds revenue
Spending and revenue are exactly equal
All taxes are automatically abolished
rationale: Surplus revenue exceeds spending, unlike deficit/equality/abolitionofalltax. Budgetfinancial sense checked. No assertion surplus means government has no existing debt.

prompt: What does the public sector include?
answers: Organisations owned or controlled by government
Only privately owned businesses
Only foreign political parties
Only independent family firms
rationale: Public sector government owned/controlled organisations. Privatelyownedbusinesses,foreignparties,independentfamilyfirms not defining. No claim every publicly accessible shop is public sector.

prompt: What does nationalisation involve?
answers: Bringing an industry or business into public ownership
Selling a state-owned business to private owners
Moving powers from national to regional government
Changing the citizenship rules for workers
rationale: Nationalisation moves industry into public ownership. Oppositeprivatisation,devolution,citizenshiprulechange different. British spelling nationalisation retained though dictionary URLAmerican nationalization.

prompt: What does privatisation involve?
answers: Transferring a state-owned business into private ownership
Bringing a private company into state ownership
Moving authority from regional to central government
Extending voting rights to more people
rationale: Privatisation moves state-owned business to private ownership. Oppositenationalisation,centralisation,votingexpansion not it. British spelling; no claim every privatisation must transfer100percentatonce.

prompt: What does the idea of a welfare state involve?
answers: Public provision to support people's health and social well-being
A requirement that every public service be privately funded
A government with no social services
A system concerned only with military spending
rationale: Welfare state public health/socialprovision. No-public-services,private-onlyfunding,military-only not principle. Does not promise everyone receives identical benefits or free services in every system.

prompt: What is the civil service?
answers: The civilian administrative departments and staff of government
All candidates competing in an election
Only members of the armed forces
Only the elected cabinet ministers
rationale: Civil service civilian administrative staff/departments. Candidates,military-only,electedcabinet-only not it. Revise permanent-only wording because fixed-term civilian staff exist; relevant administrative senses checked.

prompt: What does an ombudsman generally investigate?
answers: Complaints about organisations or public administration
The results of every public opinion poll
The military strategy of every country
The selection of every election candidate
rationale: Ombudsman investigates complaints about organisations/administration. Pollresults,globalmilitarystrategy,allcandidate selection not job. Generally allows public/private schemes; no binding powers claimed universally.

prompt: What does deputy mean in a political job title?
answers: Someone authorised to act for or assist a more senior official
Someone automatically entitled to inherit a throne
